syntheses.title: Lack of Direct Comparison of End-to-End CNN and Mid-Level RNN Approaches in Autonomous Driving
syntheses.body: The claims describe two distinct autonomous driving methods: an end-to-end CNN approach that learns the entire processing pipeline to steer a car (claim e66d15a0-9347-5814-b053-1ff1dea8058d from paper A) and a mid-level input/output RNN approach that outputs driving trajectories (claim cc49c2d4-b50d-5322-8525-304268249b24 from paper B). However, there is no claim providing a direct empirical comparison or evaluation of these two methods under the same conditions or datasets. This indicates a gap in the literature regarding how these fundamentally different architectures perform relative to each other in autonomous driving tasks.

syntheses.title: Insufficient Evidence on Effectiveness of Pure Imitation Learning Despite Large Datasets and Mid-Level Representations
syntheses.body: Claims from paper B indicate that pure imitation learning is insufficient even with 30 million examples and mid-level input/output representations (claim 639f88c8-001d-587a-bae9-390fb3c89dcf), and that closed-loop operation causes error accumulation and distribution shift (claim c9759883-dd81-58a9-ab2d-155a512245df). While paper A uses large datasets and end-to-end CNN training (claims 1f44da23-b078-5b48-9c3b-0f7f3315f522, 5b04c50f-7b96-5ddd-a0be-8eb2d45b4a96), there is no claim addressing whether end-to-end approaches overcome the limitations of pure imitation learning identified in paper B. This points to a gap in understanding the comparative effectiveness of imitation learning approaches and how to mitigate their limitations.
